title: Images, Layers & Dockerfiles
objectives: Explain the layer/cache model and order Dockerfile instructions to keep builds fast
Write a multi-stage Dockerfile that ships a small, non-root Node API image
Choose between volume and bind mount for state and live editing
Describe what a container filesystem actually is (image layers + writable layer)
body:
Works on my machine dies the moment the second machine appears: a teammate's laptop, CI, production. A container image freezes the runtime — OS libraries, Node version, your code — into one artifact that runs identically everywhere. The skill is building images that are small, fast to rebuild, and safe to run.

## The problem

A naive Dockerfile for a Node API copies everything, installs on every build, runs as root, and lands at 1.2 GB. Every dependency tweak invalidates the whole cache, every deploy pushes a gigabyte, and a compromised process owns the container. Constraints: builds must be fast, images small, runtime minimal.

## The layer/cache model

Most Dockerfile instructions create a layer: a filesystem diff over the previous layer. Layers are content-addressed and shared between images, and a step's cache is reused until one of its inputs changes — after that, every later step rebuilds. This single fact dictates instruction order: things that change rarely (dependency manifests) go first, things that change always (source code) go last. `COPY package.json` + `npm ci` before `COPY . .` means editing your code no longer reinstalls dependencies.

Multi-stage builds split building from running: a fat builder stage compiles and installs; the final stage copies only the artifacts. The final image never carries dev toolchains, caches, or the secrets you used while building (they existed only in builder layers that are not shipped).

## A real Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# ---- build stage ----
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# ---- runtime stage ----
FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/health || exit 1
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

The runtime stage is one `node:22-alpine` base plus two COPY layers: ~180 MB instead of 1.2 GB, no build tools, no source. Use exec-form CMD (`["node", ...]`) so node is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly — a shell-form CMD makes `/bin/sh` PID 1, and your graceful shutdown handler never fires (see the processes lesson). USER node drops root; EXPOSE documents the port; HEALTHCHECK gives orchestrators a liveness signal.

## Images vs containers vs filesystem

An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance. Container storage = the image's read-only layers + one thin writable layer, discarded with the container unless you mount a volume. Anything written to /tmp inside a container is gone after `docker rm` — which is why databases get volumes.

## Volumes vs bind mounts

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16   # managed, portable
docker run -v "$PWD/src:/app/src" node:22 npm test          # live-edit local code
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapi                    # harden the writable layer
```

Volumes are Docker-managed (named, portable, survive container removal) — the default for stateful data. Bind mounts map a host directory in — the default for development (edit on the host, container sees it instantly) and a footgun in production (host coupling, path drift, permission mismatches).

## Tags

`node:22-alpine` pins the major and the flavor but still floats within it; `latest` is a lie that means 'whatever was pushed last'. Production pins more precisely — at minimum a full version, ideally a digest: `node@sha256:...`. Reproducibility is a pinning decision, made at build time.

## Best practices

- Order: manifests → dependency install → source copy → build. Maximize cache hits.
- Multi-stage: compile heavy, ship light; copy artifacts with COPY --from.
- Run as a non-root USER; one process per container; log to stdout/stderr.
- .dockerignore node_modules, .git, tests, .env before your first build.
- Pin base images to versions or digests; never deploy :latest.
- Give stateful data a named volume; keep bind mounts in dev only.

## Common mistakes

- COPY . . before installing dependencies — every code edit reinstalls the world.
- Secrets in RUN lines or COPYed .env files — layer history keeps them forever, even in 'deleted later' files.
- Shell-form CMD wrapping your app in a shell and swallowing SIGTERM.
- Building a 1.5 GB image with dev dependencies, then wondering why deploys crawl.
- Storing database files in the container's writable layer and losing them at the next recreate.

examples.name: Dockerfile
examples.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

########## stage 1: build ##########
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app

# 1) manifests first: this layer caches until package*.json changes
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

# 2) source last: changes often, invalidates only the build layer
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

########## stage 2: runtime ##########
FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    PORT=3000
WORKDIR /app

# copy ONLY artifacts from the builder
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist

# never root; exec-form CMD so SIGTERM reaches node
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s \
  CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/health || exit 1
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

########## build & run (comments) ##########
# docker build -t myapi:1.4.2 .
# docker run -p 3000:3000 myapi:1.4.2
# .dockerignore should contain: node_modules, .git, .env, tests

exercise.prompt: Cache-sense trainer: each line of a Dockerfile is either CACHE-HIT (early, rarely-changing instruction) or CACHE-BUST (late, frequently-changing instruction). Write classifyLines(lines) that returns one { line, verdict } per line plus a one-line reason, then render the verdict list. Order of instructions decides the verdict — explain each in terms of what changed.
hints: Base image, WORKDIR, dependency manifests and the install rarely change -> CACHE-HIT.
COPY . . (source code) changes on every edit -> CACHE-BUST, and everything after it rebuilds.
CMD does not execute at build time, so it stays cheap even at the end.

questions.prompt: You edit one source file and rebuild. With COPY package*.json → RUN npm ci → COPY . . ordering, what happens?
options: npm ci runs again because the file tree changed
Dependency layers come from cache; only the source COPY and later steps rebuild
The whole image rebuilds from scratch
Docker refuses to build because of the change
questions.explanation: The cache invalidates starting at the first changed instruction. package*.json is unchanged, so the manifest COPY and npm ci layers are reused; only COPY . . and after rebuild.

questions.prompt: A teammate stores DB files by writing them inside the container's writable layer. What happens?
options: They persist forever — containers are permanent
They are lost when the container is removed; use a volume instead
They automatically sync to the registry
They make the image larger after each run
questions.explanation: The writable layer dies with the container. Persistent data belongs in a named volume (or bind mount in dev), which survives container removal.

questions.prompt: Why do multi-stage builds produce smaller, safer runtime images?
options: Build toolchains and build-time secrets stay in the builder stage; runtime copies only artifacts
They skip the OS layer entirely
They force images to be read-only
questions.explanation: The final stage starts from a clean base and copies only what runs (node_modules, dist). Compilers, caches and any secrets used during build never ship.
